title: sync: Mutex, RWMutex & WaitGroup
summary: The `sync` package guards shared memory. A **Mutex** gives one goroutine exclusive access to a critical section; an **RWMutex** allows many concurrent readers OR one writer; a **WaitGroup** waits for a set of goroutines to finish. They're the lock-based complement to channels: 'share memory by communicating' OR, when you must share state, protect it.

subtopics.title: Mutex: mutual exclusion
subtopics.explanation: A sync.Mutex has Lock() and Unlock(). Only one goroutine can hold the lock at a time; others block at Lock() until it's released. The code between Lock and Unlock is the critical section that touches shared state.

subtopics.title: Always unlock (use defer)
subtopics.explanation: Pair every Lock with an Unlock, and prefer defer mu.Unlock() right after locking so the lock is released even if the function returns early or panics. Forgetting to unlock deadlocks every future Lock.

subtopics.title: Data races
subtopics.explanation: A data race is two goroutines accessing the same memory concurrently with at least one write and no synchronization. Results are undefined and may corrupt data. Run tests with go test -race to detect them.
subtopics.example: // go run -race main.go reports the race

subtopics.title: RWMutex: many readers or one writer
subtopics.explanation: sync.RWMutex adds RLock()/RUnlock() for readers. Any number of readers can hold the read lock simultaneously, but a writer's Lock() excludes all readers and other writers. Use it when reads vastly outnumber writes.

subtopics.title: WaitGroup: awaiting completion
subtopics.explanation: A sync.WaitGroup is a counter: Add(n) before launching, Done() (deferred) inside each goroutine, Wait() blocks until the count hits zero. Add must run before the goroutine could call Done, or Wait may return too early.
subtopics.example: wg.Add(1); go func(){ defer wg.Done(); work() }(); wg.Wait()

subtopics.title: Zero-value ready, never copy
subtopics.explanation: A zero-value Mutex/RWMutex/WaitGroup is ready to use — no constructor needed. But you must NOT copy one after first use (pass by pointer); copying duplicates its internal state and breaks mutual exclusion. go vet catches lock copies.
subtopics.example: type Counter struct{ mu sync.Mutex; n int } // embed, pass *Counter

foundations.overview: Channels are Go's preferred way to coordinate goroutines, but sometimes goroutines genuinely share a piece of state — a counter, a cache, a map — and you need to protect it. The sync package provides locks for exactly that. A Mutex enforces that only one goroutine at a time runs a critical section; an RWMutex relaxes that to allow many simultaneous readers when there's no writer; and a WaitGroup lets one goroutine wait for a group of others to finish. Used correctly, they eliminate data races; used carelessly, they create deadlocks.
foundations.formalDefinition: sync.Mutex is a mutual-exclusion lock with Lock/Unlock that serializes access to a critical section. sync.RWMutex is a reader/writer lock permitting concurrent RLock holders but exclusive Lock for writers. sync.WaitGroup is a counter (Add/Done/Wait) used to block until a collection of goroutines completes.
foundations.whyItMatters: Any time goroutines write shared memory, you need synchronization or you have a data race — undefined behavior that corrupts data and causes flaky, hard-to-reproduce bugs. Knowing when to lock, which lock to use, and how to avoid deadlocks is fundamental to correct concurrent Go and a core interview area.
foundations.mentalModel: A Mutex is the single key to a small room: whoever holds it is inside alone; everyone else waits at the door. An RWMutex is a library reading room: many people can read at once, but to reshelve (write) the room must be cleared. A WaitGroup is a tally clicker at the exit that the supervisor watches until it reads zero.
foundations.runtimePerspective: A Mutex starts as a cheap atomic compare-and-swap on a fast path; only under contention does it fall back to parking the goroutine via the runtime's semaphore, and it has a starvation-avoidance mode that hands the lock to long-waiting goroutines. RWMutex tracks a reader count and a writer flag. None of these spin-wait at the user level.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Protecting in-memory counters and caches, guarding a shared map (or use sync.Map), serializing access to a connection or buffer, and waiting for a batch of concurrent operations with a WaitGroup.
foundations.businessImpact: Eliminating data races prevents silent data corruption and the costly, intermittent outages it causes. Choosing RWMutex for read-heavy workloads improves throughput, directly affecting latency and capacity.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Correct locking keeps shared-state code provably safe and reviewable; the -race detector turns a whole class of subtle bugs into CI failures. Misuse, though, introduces deadlocks and lock-copy bugs.
foundations.performanceImpact: Uncontended locks are very cheap (an atomic op); heavy contention serializes goroutines and tanks throughput. RWMutex helps read-heavy paths but its bookkeeping makes it slower than a plain Mutex when writes are frequent or critical sections are tiny.
commonUseCases: Protecting a shared counter or accumulator
Guarding a read-heavy in-memory cache with RWMutex
Serializing writes to a shared map
Waiting for a batch of goroutines with WaitGroup

commonMisconceptions.myth: A data race just gives a wrong value occasionally.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A data race is undefined behavior — it can corrupt memory, tear values, or crash; never reason about its 'usual' outcome.

commonMisconceptions.myth: RWMutex is always faster than Mutex.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only when reads dominate and critical sections are non-trivial; its extra bookkeeping can make it slower than a plain Mutex otherwise.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can copy a struct containing a sync.Mutex.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Copying a used lock duplicates its state and breaks exclusion; pass by pointer. go vet flags lock copies.

visualExplorer.title: How a Mutex serializes goroutines
visualExplorer.caption: Two goroutines contend for one lock; the second waits at Lock() until the first Unlocks.

config.intro: Two goroutines incrementing a shared counter under a Mutex:

steps.name: G1 locks
steps.detail: Goroutine 1 calls mu.Lock() and enters the critical section; the lock is now held.

steps.name: G2 blocks
steps.detail: Goroutine 2 calls mu.Lock() but the lock is held, so it parks at the door.

steps.name: G1 mutates
steps.detail: G1 safely reads-modifies-writes the shared counter — no other goroutine can touch it.

steps.name: G1 unlocks
steps.detail: G1 calls mu.Unlock() (via defer); the runtime wakes a waiting goroutine.

steps.name: G2 proceeds
steps.detail: G2 acquires the lock and runs its critical section. The increments are serialized — no race, correct total.

visualExplorer.title: Goroutines parking on a contended lock
visualExplorer.caption: Under contention the runtime parks blocked goroutines (off the run queues) and wakes one when the lock is released, so threads aren't burned spinning.

interactiveExamples.title: A race vs a mutex-protected counter
interactiveExamples.explanation: Without a lock, 1000 goroutines incrementing count race and the total is wrong (and undefined). The Mutex serializes the read-modify-write so the final count is exactly 1000. WaitGroup waits for all of them.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: a concurrent-safe cache with RWMutex
interactiveExamples.explanation: Reads vastly outnumber writes, so RWMutex lets many Get calls run concurrently while Set is exclusive. Fill in Get and Set with the right lock methods. Using Lock for reads would needlessly serialize them.

checkpoints.prompt: With the -race detector off, what is the value of n after this runs?
checkpoints.code:
var n int
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
	wg.Add(1)
	go func() { defer wg.Done(); n++ }()
}
wg.Wait()
fmt.Println(n)
options: Some value <= 100, and the program has a data race
checkpoints.explanation: n++ is an unsynchronized read-modify-write shared across goroutines — a data race. The result is undefined and usually less than 100 because increments are lost. go test -race would flag it. Guard n with a Mutex or use sync/atomic.

options: sync.Mutex is not reentrant: locking it twice in the same goroutine deadlocks
checkpoints.explanation: Go's sync.Mutex is not reentrant. Inc holds the lock and then report tries to Lock the same mutex, which blocks forever waiting for a release that can't happen. Restructure so the locked method calls an unlocked helper, or release before calling report.

checkpoints.prompt: When is sync.RWMutex preferable to sync.Mutex?
options: When reads vastly outnumber writes and critical sections aren't trivially small
checkpoints.explanation: RWMutex lets concurrent readers proceed in parallel, which helps read-heavy workloads. Its extra bookkeeping can make it slower than a plain Mutex when writes are frequent or the critical section is tiny. Neither lock is reentrant.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line so the lock is always released, even if the function returns early.
checkpoints.explanation: defer c.mu.Unlock() right after Lock guarantees the lock is released when the function returns by any path, including a panic. A bare Unlock at the end would be skipped on an early return or panic, deadlocking future Lock calls.

codeLab.title: A concurrency-safe counter type
codeLab.instructions: Implement a `Counter` with `Inc()` and `Value() int` methods that are safe for concurrent use, then `Solve(n int) int` that launches n goroutines each calling Inc once and returns the final value. Use a sync.Mutex and a sync.WaitGroup.
hints: Embed a sync.Mutex and an int in Counter; expose Inc and Value methods that lock.
Use defer c.mu.Unlock() so the lock is released on every path.
Pass *Counter (a pointer) to goroutines — never copy a struct that holds a used lock.
Verify locally with go test -race; the test must report no data race.

debuggingLab.title: A lock that doesn't actually protect anything
debuggingLab.symptom: go vet warns 'passes lock by value', and -race still reports a race despite the mutex.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The method has a value receiver (c Counter), so each call operates on a copy of the Counter — including a copy of the Mutex. Every goroutine locks its own private mutex, so there's no mutual exclusion, and the increment mutates a throwaway copy that's discarded on return. go vet's 'passes lock by value' warning is the tell.
commonMistakes: Using a value receiver on a type that contains a sync.Mutex.
Copying a struct that embeds a lock (passing it by value).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Use a pointer receiver so all calls share the same mutex and the same underlying field.

solution.expectedOutput: (go vet clean; -race clean; increments are now serialized)

theory.question: What is a data race, and how do you prevent and detect one in Go?
theory.directAnswer: A data race is two or more goroutines accessing the same memory concurrently where at least one access is a write and there's no synchronization — its behavior is undefined. Prevent it with synchronization (a sync.Mutex, channels, or sync/atomic) so accesses don't overlap, and detect it by running tests and binaries with the -race flag.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Unsynchronized concurrent access to shared memory with at least one writer.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Goroutines share an address space; without synchronization the memory model gives no ordering guarantees.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A Mutex or channel establishes happens-before ordering; the race detector instruments memory accesses to find violations at runtime.

theory.whyImportant: Races cause silent corruption and flaky outages; recognizing and preventing them is fundamental and heavily interviewed.
theory.realWorldExample: Two handlers incrementing a shared metrics counter without a lock under-count requests and trip the race detector in CI.

followUps.question: Does -race guarantee you found all races?
followUps.answer: No — it only reports races on code paths actually exercised; thorough concurrent tests matter.

followUps.question: When is sync/atomic preferable to a Mutex?
followUps.answer: For a single word (counter, flag) where one atomic op is cheaper than locking a critical section.

theory.question: Explain sync.WaitGroup's Add/Done/Wait and the rule about where Add must be called.
theory.directAnswer: A WaitGroup is a counter: Add(n) increases it, Done() decreases it by one (usually deferred inside the goroutine), and Wait() blocks until it reaches zero. Add must be called before the goroutine could run (before the go statement), otherwise Wait() might observe zero and return before the work is counted.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A counting barrier for awaiting goroutine completion.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Goroutines don't join like threads; WaitGroup provides the join.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Add/Done adjust an internal counter; Wait parks until it's zero. A negative counter panics.

theory.whyImportant: Misplacing Add causes a race where Wait returns early — a classic, subtle bug.
theory.realWorldExample: A handler fans out N downstream calls, Add(1) before each go, defer Done() inside, Wait() before responding.

followUps.question: What happens if Done is called more times than Add?
followUps.answer: The counter goes negative and WaitGroup panics.

followUps.question: Can you reuse a WaitGroup?
followUps.answer: Yes, after Wait returns, but never call Add concurrently with a Wait that may already be at zero.

scenario.question: A service intermittently deadlocks under load; goroutine dumps show many goroutines blocked at Lock(). How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Likely a lock-ordering or reentrancy problem: either two locks are acquired in different orders by different goroutines (classic AB/BA deadlock), or a goroutine re-locks a non-reentrant mutex it already holds. Capture the goroutine pprof profile to see where they're stuck, establish a single global lock-acquisition order, never call a locking method while already holding that lock, and keep critical sections short with defer Unlock.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A deadlock from inconsistent lock ordering or non-reentrant re-locking.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: sync.Mutex isn't reentrant, and out-of-order multi-lock acquisition can cycle.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Enforcing a global lock order and avoiding nested same-lock acquisition breaks the cycle.

scenario.whyImportant: Lock-ordering deadlocks are common production incidents and a senior-level interview topic.
scenario.realWorldExample: Two methods each lock accounts A and B but in opposite orders, deadlocking when run concurrently.

followUps.question: How do you find lock contention, not just deadlocks?
followUps.answer: Use the mutex profile (runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction + pprof) to see where goroutines wait longest.

coding.question: Implement a concurrency-safe `SafeMap` with `Get`, `Set`, and `Len` using sync.RWMutex, optimized for read-heavy use.
coding.thoughtProcess: Wrap a map with an RWMutex. Reads (Get, Len) take RLock so many can run concurrently; Set takes the exclusive Lock. Use defer for every unlock to stay correct on every path, and use pointer receivers so the lock is shared (never copied).
coding.lineByLine: Get and Len use RLock/RUnlock so concurrent readers proceed in parallel — the right choice for a read-heavy map. Set uses the exclusive Lock so a writer never overlaps readers or other writers, preventing the concurrent-map-write panic and data races. Pointer receivers ensure every method shares the one RWMutex; copying it would break exclusion.

followUps.question: When would you switch from RWMutex to sync.Map?
followUps.answer: When keys are mostly written once and read many times across many goroutines, sync.Map can outperform an RWMutex-guarded map by avoiding lock contention.

followUps.question: Why does a plain map panic under concurrent writes?
followUps.answer: Go's runtime detects concurrent map writes and panics deliberately to surface the unsynchronized access.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Prefer channels for coordinating work and locks for protecting genuinely shared state. Keep critical sections small, never call out to unknown code while holding a lock, and document each lock's invariant and the data it guards.
productionDeepDive.performance: Uncontended locks are cheap; contention serializes goroutines and kills throughput. Use RWMutex for read-heavy paths, shard locks to reduce contention, and reach for sync/atomic for single-word counters and flags.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Establish a global lock-acquisition order to avoid AB/BA deadlocks, remember mutexes are not reentrant, and always run tests with -race. Pass lock-bearing types by pointer; let go vet catch lock copies.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Use defer Unlock so a panic can't leave a lock held and wedge the service. A held lock plus a panic without defer is a guaranteed future deadlock.
productionDeepDive.observability: Enable the mutex and block profiles (runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction, SetBlockProfileRate) and inspect with pprof to find contention hotspots and long waits.
productionDeepDive.security: Synchronize access to security-sensitive shared state (sessions, counters, rate-limit buckets) so races can't corrupt authorization or accounting decisions.

caseStudies.problem: Many goroutines reading a shared cache, occasional writes.
caseStudies.solution: RWMutex for concurrent reads with exclusive writes, or sync.Map for write-once/read-many keys.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: RWMutex bookkeeping vs Mutex simplicity; sync.Map's specialized API and semantics.
caseStudies.lessons: Match the lock to the read/write ratio and always verify with -race.

keyTakeaways: A sync.Mutex serializes a critical section (Lock/Unlock, always with defer); sync.RWMutex allows many readers OR one writer for read-heavy state.
A data race (concurrent access with a write and no synchronization) is undefined behavior — prevent it with locks/channels/atomics and detect it with go test -race.
sync.WaitGroup waits for goroutines: Add before launching, defer Done inside, Wait to block; Add must precede the go statement.
Mutexes are not reentrant and must never be copied after use — use pointer receivers and let go vet catch lock copies; keep critical sections short to limit contention.
